title: Proof Beyond the Pellet: Controls and Counts

scenes.visual: Title card 'Proof Beyond the Pellet: Controls and Counts' in bold white type (36 pt) fading in over a dark-slate laboratory tube scene that reuses the exact colour map from the first film: tiny warm-gold vesicles (#F5C542) with cyan interiors (#38BDF8) and coral surface ligands (#FB7185) drifting slowly among amber-grey protein clumps and lipoproteins (#D97706, #94A3B8) inside a clear tube of culture medium. Mark 'Schematic' discreetly in the bottom-right corner.

scenes.tts: The first film showed how extracellular vesicles face outward and seal cytosol inside. Yet when a centrifuge pellet changes a target cell, how can you tell a vesicle did the work? Spinning cell fluid collects far more than vesicles.
scenes.caption: The first film showed how extracellular vesicles face outward and seal cytosol inside. Yet when a centrifuge pellet changes a target cell, how can you tell a vesicle did the work? Spinning cell fluid collects far more than vesicles.
scenes.visual: Title fades cleanly. On the left, donor medium pours into a large centrifuge tube filling 70% of the frame height, teeming with gold-and-cyan vesicles alongside amber-grey protein aggregates, round grey lipoproteins, and tangled RNA–protein specks. On the right, a recipient cell glows emerald when a droplet from the tube touches it, while a large white '?' pulses between the messy mixture and the glowing cell.
scenes.narration: The first film showed how extracellular vesicles face outward and seal cytosol inside. Yet when a centrifuge pellet changes a target cell, how can you tell a vesicle did the work? Spinning cell fluid collects far more than vesicles.

scenes.tts: To collect small vesicles, researchers spin fluid at rising speeds, finishing at high speed. That spin sorts by size and density, not by identity. So the pellet also holds protein clumps, lipoproteins, R N A protein complexes and calf serum vesicles from the medium.
scenes.caption: To collect small vesicles, researchers spin fluid at rising speeds, finishing at high speed. That spin sorts by size and density, not by identity. So the pellet also holds protein clumps, lipoproteins, RNA protein complexes and calf serum vesicles from the medium.
scenes.visual: The centrifuge tube steps smoothly through three animated spin speed badges on screen ('Low: cells', 'Medium: debris', '100,000 g: small particles'). Particles stream downward into a compact mixed pellet at the bottom of the tube. Zoom into the pellet so viewers clearly see gold-and-cyan vesicles crowded tightly beside amber-grey protein clumps, lipoproteins, grey lipoproteins, tangled RNA–protein specks and pale serum vesicles ('From calf serum'). Label 'Mixed 100,000 g pellet' (28 pt).
scenes.narration: To collect small vesicles, researchers spin fluid at rising speeds, finishing at high speed. That spin sorts by size and density, not by identity. So the pellet also holds protein clumps, lipoproteins, RNA protein complexes and calf serum vesicles from the medium.

scenes.tts: Step one is separating vesicles from denser debris. Researchers load the pellet at the bottom of a dense sucrose gradient and spin until particles stop moving. Why do vesicles float upward? Membrane lipid is less dense than protein, so lipid-rich vesicles rise while free proteins stay below.
scenes.caption: Step one is separating vesicles from denser debris. Researchers load the pellet at the bottom of a dense sucrose gradient and spin until particles stop moving. Why do vesicles float upward? Membrane lipid is less dense than protein, so lipid-rich vesicles rise while free proteins stay below.
scenes.visual: The mixed pellet transfers smoothly to the very bottom of a tall sucrose gradient tube shaded from deep dense slate at the bottom to light slate at the top ('Bottom-loaded sucrose gradient', schematic). As the spin arrow rotates, buoyant gold-and-cyan vesicles float steadily upward into a mid-tube band labelled '1.13–1.19 g/mL: vesicles' (28 pt), while heavier amber-grey protein clumps remain near the bottom ('Denser: free protein').
scenes.narration: Step one is separating vesicles from denser debris. Researchers load the pellet at the bottom of a dense sucrose gradient and spin until particles stop moving. Why do vesicles float upward? Membrane lipid is less dense than protein, so lipid-rich vesicles rise while free proteins stay below.

scenes.tts: Next, test every layer on target cells, alongside a mock pellet spun from cell-free medium. If vesicles carry the signal, activity tracks the vesicle layer rather than denser protein. Even then, some lipoproteins share that buoyant zone, so separation is only the first check.
scenes.caption: Next, test every layer on target cells, alongside a mock pellet spun from cell-free medium. If vesicles carry the signal, activity tracks the vesicle layer rather than denser protein. Even then, some lipoproteins share that buoyant zone, so separation is only the first check.
scenes.visual: Droplets are drawn from the buoyant vesicle band, the dense bottom band, and a parallel 'Cell-free mock' tube onto three target-cell dishes. Emerald activity lights up under the buoyant vesicle fraction while the dense fraction and mock stay dark. A small translucent grey lipoprotein drifts into the 1.13–1.19 g/mL band with a brief tag 'Some lipoproteins overlap' so the visual stays as hedged as the narration.

scenes.tts: Step two asks whether cargo sits outside or inside the membrane. Treat the vesicles with a protease or a ribonuclease. Surface proteins get cut away, while sealed cargo survives behind the intact membrane. Adding detergent breaks the membrane, so internal cargo disappears too. One caution: bound proteins can shield loose R N A.
scenes.caption: Step two asks whether cargo sits outside or inside the membrane. Treat the vesicles with a protease or a ribonuclease. Surface proteins get cut away, while sealed cargo survives behind the intact membrane. Adding detergent breaks the membrane, so internal cargo disappears too. One caution: bound proteins can shield loose RNA.
scenes.visual: Zoom from the buoyant band into two side-by-side enlarged gold-and-cyan vesicles with coral surface proteins and cyan internal RNA strands (schematic). Left panel ('Enzyme alone'): animated scissor icons snip off the outer coral blocks while bouncing harmlessly off the intact gold ring, leaving cyan cargo untouched inside. Right panel ('Enzyme + detergent'): detergent droplets dissolve the gold ring into fragments, and scissors cut both coral and cyan cargo. In the lower corner, a small grey protein cap wraps a loose RNA strand ('Protein can shield RNA').
scenes.narration: Step two asks whether cargo sits outside or inside the membrane. Treat the vesicles with a protease or a ribonuclease. scenes.tts: Step three is counting, because tiny vesicles hold very little volume. A sphere one hundred nanometres across encloses at most about five times ten to the minus nineteen litres. Multiply that volume by one micromolar, then by Avogadro's number of molecules per mole. Passive trapping gives roughly zero point three molecules per vesicle.
scenes.caption: Step three is counting, because tiny vesicles hold very little volume. A sphere 100 nm across encloses at most about 5 × 10⁻¹⁹ L. Multiply that volume by 1 µM, then by Avogadro's number of molecules per mole. Passive trapping gives roughly 0.3 molecules per vesicle.
scenes.visual: One gold-and-cyan vesicle centres in the frame with a clean diameter bracket ('100 nm'). As each number is spoken, a readout builds beside it in 30 pt white type: 'V ≤ 5 × 10⁻¹⁹ L' (from 4/3 π r³), then '5 × 10⁻¹⁹ L × 10⁻⁶ mol/L × 6 × 10²³ /mol', then '≈ 0.3 molecules / vesicle'. Three vesicles appear in a row, with only one tiny glowing cyan dot appearing inside one of the three—visually making '0.3 per vesicle' intuitive while dozens of coral ligands stud each vesicle's outer gold rim.
scenes.narration: Step three is counting, because tiny vesicles hold very little volume. A sphere 100 nm across encloses at most about 5 × 10⁻¹⁹ L. Multiply that volume by 1 µM, then by Avogadro's number of molecules per mole. Passive trapping gives roughly 0.3 molecules per vesicle.

scenes.tts: Copies per vesicle equals cargo copies divided by particles counted. Suppose a purified sample holds two billion vesicles and forty million copies of one micro R N A. Does the average vesicle hold many copies, about one copy, or far less than one?
scenes.caption: Copies per vesicle equals cargo copies divided by particles counted. Suppose a purified sample holds two billion vesicles and forty million copies of one micro RNA. Does the average vesicle hold many copies, about one copy, or far less than one?
scenes.visual: The formula appears large and clear at the top (30 pt): 'copies per vesicle = copies ÷ particles'. Below it, two clean counters fill smoothly as spoken: '40,000,000 copies' in cyan over '2,000,000,000 vesicles' in gold. Beneath the division bar, three choice chips glow softly: 'Many', 'About 1', 'Far less than 1', with a pulsing '?' beside the equals sign.
scenes.narration: Copies per vesicle equals cargo copies divided by particles counted. Suppose a purified sample holds two billion vesicles and forty million copies of one micro RNA. Does the average vesicle hold many copies, about one copy, or far less than one?

scenes.visual: Hold the equation '40,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000,000 = ?' and the three options ('Many', 'About 1', 'Far less than 1') on screen while vesicles drift gently in the background and a subtle progress bar glides across the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: Far less than one, because forty million divided by two billion is zero point zero two. That is just one copy in every fifty vesicles. Counts in real samples also put a given micro R N A far below one copy per vesicle. A vesicle surface, by contrast, displays many ligand copies.
scenes.caption: Far less than one, because forty million divided by two billion is zero point zero two. That is just one copy in every fifty vesicles. Counts in real samples also put a given micro RNA far below one copy per vesicle. A vesicle surface, by contrast, displays many ligand copies.
scenes.visual: The 'Far less than 1' chip illuminates emerald; the equation completes as each piece is spoken: '40,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000,000 = 0.02' -> '1 copy in 50 vesicles'. A neat 5×10 grid of 50 tiny gold vesicle rings populates the lower half of the frame: 49 have empty dark interiors and only 1 glows with a single cyan microRNA dot, while coral surface ligands glint brightly around the outer rim of a zoomed vesicle beside the grid.
scenes.narration: Far less than one, because forty million divided by two billion is zero point zero two. That is just one copy in every fifty vesicles. Counts in real samples also put a given micro RNA far below one copy per vesicle. A vesicle surface, by contrast, displays many ligand copies.

scenes.tts: Low averages do not rule out internal signalling, since a rare subset might carry most copies. They mean any claim needs realistic doses and honest controls. Proving vesicle signalling requires separating vesicles, locating cargo, and counting copies.

scenes.visual: In the 50-vesicle grid, a brief subtle glow highlights one rare vesicle holding several cyan dots ('Rare subset?'), then the frame pulls back to display the three completed verification icons side by side in crisp high contrast: (1) buoyant sucrose gradient band ('Separate vesicles'), (2) protease/RNase ± detergent vesicle ('Locate cargo'), and (3) copies ÷ particles counter ('Count copies'), with a steady emerald checkmark beneath all three.

scenes.visual: Clean dark-slate end card with one single centred line in crisp white type (32 pt), nothing underneath it, over a faint slowly drifting gold-and-cyan vesicle outline: 'Proving vesicle signalling requires separating vesicles, locating cargo, and counting copies.'
